content: 1. The evidence regarding the effectiveness of impermeable gowns compared to surgical gowns or coveralls in preventing virus transmission to healthcare workers is of very low quality. There is no comparative evidence available, and no estimate of effectiveness can be made. 2. The certainty of evidence for the prevention of personal well-being issues, such as heat stress, dehydration, hyperthermia, heat stroke, presyncope, and syncope, when using impermeable gowns versus surgical gowns or coveralls, is also very low. No comparative evidence exists, and no effectiveness estimate can be provided. 3. The evidence on the impact of impermeable gowns on dexterity, the ability to perform procedures and tasks, and overall functionality is of very low quality. There is no comparative evidence, and no estimate of effectiveness is available. 4. A simulation study assessed viral self-contamination after healthcare workers performed a 16-step Ebola virus PPE doffing protocol. Participants were assigned to either additional glove sanitization using hypochlorite spray or alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR). The study found no detectable transfer of enveloped bacteriophage Φ6 to participants, but the certainty of evidence comparing hypochlorite spray and ABHR for preventing Φ6 transfer was judged to be very low. 5. Additional glove sanitization with hypochlorite was found to have low certainty of evidence in preventing the transfer of MS2 compared to ABHR. 6. A retrospective cohort study evaluated the level of Ebola virus IgG antibodies and prior exposure events among responders to the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic. The study collected data on PPE use, including whether PPE removal was performed with or without chlorine spray. However, the data was deemed unreliable due to collinearity between the use of spray and healthcare worker roles. 7. Almost all participants performing clinical work used chlorine spray, while those not using spray were primarily involved in laboratory work. This occupational difference in exposure likelihood made it impossible to analyze the independent effect of spraying PPE with chlorine. 8. The overall certainty of evidence for the effectiveness of spraying PPE with chlorine prior to removal to mitigate the risk of Ebola virus transmission was judged to be very low. 9. A review of contextual information identified 13 studies describing doffing protocols. None of these protocols included a discrete step for spraying PPEs with chlorine. Common themes included the risk of self-contamination during doffing, even among experienced healthcare workers, and the need for careful handling of scrubs and effective hand hygiene. 10. During PPE doffing, common protocol deviations included touching outer gloves with inner-gloved hands and touching the outside of gloves with bare hands. Hand hygiene and glove removal were identified as high-risk opportunities for self-contamination. 11. Optimizing doffing protocols may require reinforcing careful handling of scrubs and ensuring good glove/hand hygiene with effective agents. Hands-free alcohol-based hand rub dispensers that remain uncontaminated may also be beneficial. 12. The risk of bias in the studies was judged to be moderate using the ROBINS-I tool for non-randomized studies. Most domains were rated as low risk, except for one domain, which was rated as moderate risk due to the lack of blinding of participants and the trained monitor guiding participants through the doffing process. 13. The evidence for the transfer of surrogate viruses (MS2 and Φ6) to inner gloves, hands, face, or scrubs following doffing protocols was based on data from a single observational study with 15 participants. The certainty of evidence was very low due to serious indirectness and imprecision. 14. A total of 250 studies were screened, but none met the eligibility criteria for appropriate interventions and comparators. However, evidence addressing hand hygiene protocols for healthcare workers handling highly infectious diseases was noted. 15. A simulation study compared contamination levels when handwashing with soap and water was performed before/after each PPE doffing step versus when glove removal was followed by handwashing. The study highlighted the importance of hand hygiene in reducing contamination risks. 16. A Cochrane systematic review included evidence on simulated contamination for ABHR versus no glove sanitization. The findings emphasized the need for effective hand hygiene protocols. 17. Wolfe et al. conducted a randomized trial to evaluate skin irritation caused by frequent handwashing during Ebola outbreaks. They found that sanitizer caused the least irritation, followed by high-pH chlorine solutions, soap and water, and neutral-pH chlorine solutions. The study recommended using the most acceptable, available, and sustainable handwashing methods in outbreak settings. 18. Another study evaluated the effectiveness of 0.05% chlorine solutions in inactivating and removing model organisms (Φ6 and E. coli) from hands. High-test hypochlorite (HTH) performed consistently well, with significant reductions in organisms compared to other protocols. However, the differences in efficacy were small, suggesting similar effectiveness across protocols. 19. Overall, the authors recommend using the most practical handwashing method to ensure hand hygiene in Ebola and Marburg disease contexts, considering the benefits and drawbacks of each method.
